openingProblem.problem: Between 1990 and 1994 some 15,000 people died in political violence, yet in April 1994 nearly twenty million people voted peacefully in a 'free and fair' election. How did a country on the edge of civil war negotiate its way to democracy?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: what held the negotiations together?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Talks about talks, 1990–1992
chunks.body:
De Klerk's announcement of **2 February 1990** opened the way to negotiation, but a peaceful outcome was far from certain. It took four years of negotiations and some **15,000 deaths** in political violence before a settlement was reached. The two main sides had conflicting visions. The ANC wanted majority rule and a constitution drawn up by an elected constituent assembly. The government wanted power-sharing that would protect "minority interests" and a leading role for the National Party in writing the new constitution.

Talks began in Cape Town in May 1990 and produced the **Groote Schuur Minute**, a commitment to further negotiations. In the **Pretoria Minute** of August 1990 the ANC agreed to suspend the armed struggle and the government lifted the state of emergency. De Klerk's government also repealed the remaining apartheid laws, including the Group Areas Act and the Population Registration Act.

Formal negotiations began in December 1991 at the **Convention for a Democratic South Africa** (CODESA). Nearly 300 delegates from nineteen political groupings attended, but the ANC and the National Party dominated, through their chief negotiators Cyril Ramaphosa and Roelf Meyer. Parties on the extremes, the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC) on the left and the Conservative Party on the right, boycotted the talks. CODESA agreed on a two-stage process: an interim constitution, then a final constitution drawn up by the first elected parliament.

De Klerk faced a revolt from conservatives in his own party. In 1992 he held a referendum among white voters, and **69 per cent** voted to continue reform. The result made the National Party more confident, and it took a tougher line at CODESA, demanding special protection for minorities and a coalition government.

This mattered because both sides wanted a settlement but on very different terms, which meant that negotiation was always vulnerable to a breakdown in trust.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Pretoria Minute ended the armed struggle and the state of emergency.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Talks took place amid mutual suspicion.

argumentsThatWork.claim: CODESA brought most parties to the table.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The PAC and the Conservative Party boycotted it.
It also made the NP harder to negotiate with.

chunks.title: Violence and breakthrough, 1992–1994
chunks.body:
Violence threatened the process throughout. Rivalry between the ANC and the Zulu nationalist **Inkatha Freedom Party** caused much of it, and many suspected a sinister "Third Force" of security personnel secretly stirring up conflict. In May 1992 the ANC broke off negotiations. In June, at **Boipatong**, Inkatha supporters helped by the police attacked ANC members attending a funeral, killing dozens. Mandela suspended talks. The Goldstone Report later confirmed police involvement and the existence of a Third Force. The ANC, SACP and COSATU launched "rolling mass action", and in September 1992 soldiers in the Ciskei homeland fired on unarmed protesters at **Bisho**.

Bisho persuaded both sides that talks had to resume. In September 1992 they signed a **Record of Understanding**. The government released more political prisoners and banned "traditional weapons" at Inkatha rallies. The ANC accepted a Government of National Unity including the National Party for five years, and agreed to honour the contracts of civil servants, judges, police and soldiers. These **"sunset clauses"**, proposed by the SACP leader Joe Slovo, provided the crucial breakthrough. Historians disagree about the turning point: Leonard Thompson sees the Record of Understanding as the moment Mandela gained the upper hand over De Klerk; Giliomee and Mbenga point to Boipatong.

The violence went on. In April 1993 **Chris Hani**, a popular MK, ANC and SACP leader, was assassinated by Janusz Walus with a gun supplied by a Conservative Party member. Mandela's televised appeal for calm on 10 April defused the crisis. White extremists of the AWB stormed the World Trade Centre in June 1993 and, shortly before the election, 5,000 armed AWB members invaded the homeland of Bophuthatswana. The PAC's armed wing attacked a church congregation in Cape Town. Inkatha's leader, Buthelezi, threatened to boycott the election.

Even so, in November 1993 the negotiators agreed an **interim constitution**, and a Transitional Executive Council oversaw the run-up to the election. One week before the vote, Inkatha agreed to take part.

This mattered because each crisis pushed the main parties closer together rather than apart, which meant that violence delayed the settlement but did not destroy it.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Each crisis was followed by renewed talks.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The sunset clauses were the crucial breakthrough.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Giliomee and Mbenga see Boipatong as the turning point.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Mandela's leadership defused the Hani crisis.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Mandela had also suspended talks after Boipatong.

chunks.title: Election and a new constitution, 1994–1996
chunks.body:
From 27 to 29 April 1994 nearly **twenty million** people, most of whom had never voted before, took part in South Africa's first election based on universal suffrage. Despite the violence that preceded it, the vote was remarkably peaceful, and foreign observers declared it "free and fair". The ANC won **62.65 per cent**, the National Party 20.39 per cent and Inkatha 10.54 per cent. The National Party won the Western Cape and Inkatha narrowly won KwaZulu-Natal.

Under the sunset clause, every party with at least 5 per cent of the vote joined a **Government of National Unity** for five years: twelve ANC ministers, six from the National Party and three from Inkatha. De Klerk and Thabo Mbeki served as deputy presidents, and Buthelezi became minister of home affairs. The government had to rebuild the state: the homelands were absorbed into nine new provinces, and a new defence force integrated MK and APLA guerrillas with the old army.

The elected parliament sat as a **Constitutional Assembly**, chaired by Cyril Ramaphosa, from May 1994 to May 1996. It received 1.7 million written submissions from the public. The **1996 constitution** created a National Assembly of 400 members and a National Council of Provinces, with elections every five years by proportional representation from party lists. Amendments needed a two-thirds majority. A comprehensive **Bill of Rights** listed economic as well as civil and political rights, and copies were distributed in all eleven official languages. A **Constitutional Court** protected the constitution: in its first case it abolished the death penalty, and in 1999 it ruled that prisoners had the right to vote. The historian Tom Lodge suggests one weakness: because party leaders controlled the lists, ANC MPs were reluctant to question government policy.

This mattered because the constitution was negotiated, popular and protected by an independent court, which meant that South Africa's democracy rested on firm legal foundations.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The 1994 election was free, fair and peaceful.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: There were doubts about procedures in KwaZulu-Natal.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Government of National Unity shared power.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The ANC held a clear majority of ministers.
Lodge argues the list system weakened parliament.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The 1996 constitution protected democracy through rights and an independent court.

useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that citizens could challenge the government in court, so power was limited by law.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Tom Lodge argues that the party list system made ANC MPs reluctant to question government policy.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The constitution therefore protected rights strongly, while weakening parliament's check on the executive.

chunks.title: A dominant-party democracy, 1996–1999
chunks.body:
Shortly after the constitution was adopted, the Government of National Unity broke up. In **May 1996** the National Party withdrew, claiming it had little influence as a minority partner and wanted to form a strong opposition. De Klerk stepped down as deputy president and retired from party politics in 1997. The party re-formed as the New National Party but struggled to attract support. Historians explain its collapse differently: Leonard Thompson argues the new constitution was the final straw, because it made no provision for power-sharing after 1999; Nigel Worden blames De Klerk's miscalculation; Hermann Giliomee thinks the Truth and Reconciliation Commission hearings "probably destroyed" the party.

Inkatha stayed in government, and the violence between its supporters and the ANC's subsided. In 1997 **Thabo Mbeki** took over the ANC leadership, and in the **1999 election** the ANC increased its support to **66.36 per cent**, winning 266 of the 400 seats. The Democratic Party, with less than 10 per cent, became the official opposition. Party politics remained largely split along racial lines. As president from 1999, Mbeki shifted the focus from reconciliation to transformation.

Was South Africa a working democracy? Thompson calls it a "one-party democracy", but stresses strong checks on the abuse of power: a free press, a vigorous civil society, and powerful business organisations and trade unions. The political scientist David Welsh notes that, though a single dominant party had become entrenched, democratic constitutional forms had been maintained.

This mattered because democracy survived its first transfer of power from Mandela to Mbeki, which meant that the constitution worked even though no party could seriously challenge the ANC.

argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Opposition parties were small and fragmented.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Democracy had strong checks despite ANC dominance.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The National Party declined because the new order gave it no special role.
useItInAnEssay.prove: It withdrew from the Government of National Unity in May 1996, and Thompson argues the constitution was the final straw because it made no provision for power-sharing after 1999.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the NP lost its influence and many supporters, so in 1999 the Democratic Party replaced it as the official opposition.

useItInAnEssay.judge: The NP's decline therefore left the ANC dominant, creating what Thompson calls a 'one-party democracy'.

This meant that the ANC stayed committed to negotiation, so the process survived the violence.
However, De Klerk began the process and won the 1992 referendum, and Slovo's sunset clauses provided the crucial breakthrough.
Mandela was therefore the most important individual, though the settlement needed several leaders willing to compromise.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the success of the Government of National Unity between 1994 and 1996.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge

modelPlan.thesis: The GNU succeeded in its main goal, a negotiated constitution with wide participation, but failed as a lasting coalition, since the National Party withdrew in 1996.
modelPlan.counter: The NP claimed it had little influence, which suggests power-sharing was more formal than real.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Judged by its main goal, a constitution, the GNU was a success.

segments.text: The Government of National Unity succeeded in its main task, though not as a lasting coalition.
Its Constitutional Assembly, chaired by Ramaphosa, received 1.7 million submissions and adopted the final constitution in May 1996.
This meant that South Africa gained a constitution with wide public support, so democracy rested on firm foundations.
However, in May 1996 the National Party withdrew, claiming it had little influence as a minority partner.
The GNU was therefore a success, because it achieved the constitution before power-sharing broke down.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Discuss the causes and effects of the decline of the National Party between 1996 and 1999.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: weigh the causes and effects, then judge
decodeKey.scope: The decline of the National Party
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which effect was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The National Party declined because the new constitution gave it no guaranteed role after 1999 and the TRC damaged its reputation; the main effect was the ANC's dominance in a 'one-party democracy'.

arguments.claim: Cause: De Klerk's miscalculation and the TRC.
Effect: withdrawal from the GNU and the NNP.

modelPlan.counter: Thompson notes strong checks on the ANC, which suggests the NP's decline did not end democracy.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which cause mattered most? The constitution, which ended guaranteed power-sharing.

segments.text: The National Party declined because the new order gave it no guaranteed role.
It withdrew from the GNU in May 1996, and Thompson argues the constitution was the final straw because it made no provision for power-sharing after 1999.
This meant that the NP could only be a minority opposition, so many supporters moved to the Democratic Party, which became the official opposition in 1999.
However, Giliomee argues the TRC hearings 'probably destroyed' the party, and Worden blames De Klerk's miscalculation.
The most significant effect was therefore the ANC's dominance, which Thompson calls a 'one-party democracy'.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the ways in which the 1996 constitution protected democracy in South Africa between 1996 and 1999.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: Which protection mattered most, and any weakness

modelPlan.thesis: The 1996 constitution protected democracy through a Bill of Rights, a Constitutional Court and proportional elections, though the party-list system weakened parliament's check on the government.

arguments.claim: Proportional representation and the amendment rule.
Limits: the list system and ANC dominance.

modelPlan.counter: Tom Lodge argues the list system weakened parliamentary democracy.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which protection mattered most? The Constitutional Court, which could overrule parliament.

segments.text: The 1996 constitution protected democracy chiefly through an independent Constitutional Court.
The court could strike down unconstitutional laws; it abolished the death penalty in its first case and in 1999 ruled that prisoners had the right to vote.
This meant that citizens could enforce their rights against the government, so power was limited by law.
However, Tom Lodge argues that the party-list system made ANC MPs reluctant to question government policy.
The constitution therefore protected rights strongly, while leaving parliament weaker than the courts.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the significance of the Record of Understanding for the negotiations between 1992 and 1994.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The significance of the Record of Understanding
decodeKey.judgement: Turning point, or one step among several?

modelPlan.thesis: The Record of Understanding was the turning point of the negotiations, because Slovo's sunset clauses reconciled majority rule with temporary power-sharing; but violence continued, and Giliomee and Mbenga see Boipatong as the real shift in power.

arguments.claim: The road to the interim constitution.

modelPlan.counter: Violence continued into 1994, with Hani's assassination and the AWB.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Was it the turning point? Yes for agreement; Boipatong may have shifted power first.

segments.text: The Record of Understanding was the turning point in the negotiations.
Signed in September 1992 after Bisho, it committed the ANC to a five-year Government of National Unity and protected civil servants' jobs through Slovo's sunset clauses.
This meant that white fears were reduced, so the National Party could accept elections, and Thompson sees it as the moment Mandela gained the upper hand.
However, Giliomee and Mbenga argue that Boipatong was the turning point, and violence continued with Hani's assassination in 1993.
The Record of Understanding was therefore significant as the moment agreement became possible.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the constitutional changes made in South Africa and Argentina between 1993 and 1996.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences throughout
decodeKey.judgement: How far did each change strengthen democracy?

modelPlan.thesis: Both states changed their constitutions through agreements between rival parties and both strengthened the protection of rights, but South Africa wrote an entirely new constitution with mass participation to create democracy, whereas Argentina amended an existing one, partly to allow its president a second term.

arguments.claim: Difference: a new constitution with public participation versus an amendment.
Difference: purpose: founding democracy versus re-election and limits on power.

modelPlan.counter: Argentina's reform also limited presidential power, through a Council of Magistracy and a shorter term.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which change did more for democracy? South Africa's, because it created democratic rights for the majority for the first time.

segments.text: South Africa and Argentina both used negotiated constitutional change to strengthen democracy, but for different purposes.

South Africa's 1996 constitution, drafted by an elected Constitutional Assembly that received 1.7 million submissions, created a Bill of Rights, whereas Argentina's 1994 amendment, agreed by Menem and Alfonsín in the Pact of Olivos, gave human rights treaties constitutional status.
This meant that both constitutions protected rights more strongly, but South Africa's founded a democracy for the whole population, while Argentina's reformed an existing democracy.
However, Argentina's amendment was driven partly by Menem's wish for re-election, while South Africa's process was driven by the need to replace apartheid.
The two changes were therefore similar in method but different in scale: South Africa's was a refoundation, Argentina's a renegotiation.
